source.title: A Geometric View for Understanding Concept Learning and Neuron Interpretation in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Chen-Hao Zhang; Chris Lin; Su-In Lee

record.tranche_reason: The paper tests SAE concept-learning capacity and single-neuron versus multi-neuron representations on synthetic data, using set-alignment and F1 measures rather than the original Toy Models of Superposition method.
record.gate_note: The reported synthetic SAE results and capacity theorem bear on representational capacity and polysemanticity. The paper also reports disagreement-ratio results; these measure whether concept learning and neuron interpretation agree, not whether features are overlapping directions or canonical units. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: No version is tested. The paper trains ReLU and Top-K SAEs directly on 2-D synthetic point clusters, where each human concept is a cluster in input space. It then measures how well single SAE neurons or intersections of neurons (units) align with those clusters, scored by F1. No network is trained under capacity pressure, and nothing is measured about how a model's own neurons or directions store sparse features: no superposition geometry, no feature importance, no polysemanticity of a model's neurons. The SAE is the object studied as an interpretation tool, and the paper reports how its own set-alignment framework performs. The capacity result (Theorem 5.10) is a counting bound derived for SAE monosemanticity, not an empirical result about superposition. The findings are SAE concept-alignment results, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors frame concepts as sets and concept learning as set alignment, and argue that single neurons are often insufficient. They hold that wider SAEs help by supplying more candidate features, that excessive sparsity can hurt, and that concept learning and neuron interpretation need not agree. They add that the experiments are 2-D synthetic illustrations of the theory and that the empirical study of disagreement is preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Uses trained ReLU and Top-K SAEs on two-dimensional synthetic concept clusters, evaluates concept-set alignment and F1, and studies multi-neuron units and concept interpretation. It does not reproduce the original Toy Models of Superposition procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with SAE expansion factor, L0, concept overlap and geometry, ReLU versus Top-K gating, and the exact number of selected neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: On 2-D synthetic clusters, single SAE neurons often fail to align with non-convex-separable concepts. Intersections of 3–5 neurons raise F1 substantially (e.g. 0.4144 to 0.8529 for ReLU; 0.4559 to 0.9646 for Top-K), and heavily overlapping concepts remain hard.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Human concepts that are not linearly separable are better captured by intersections of several SAE latents than by any single latent.

fits_no_version.finding: Best concept F1 rises with SAE expansion factor up to about 16, then plateaus. Disjoint concepts reach higher F1 than overlapping ones.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider SAEs improve alignment with ground-truth concepts up to a plateau, with weaker gains for overlapping concepts.

fits_no_version.finding: A theoretical counting bound: SAE width must satisfy roughly d ≳ (kc!|C|)^(1/kc) for perfect monosemanticity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The SAE width needed for monosemantic units scales with the number of concepts and the per-concept neuron budget.

fits_no_version.finding: The aggregate disagreement between the concept-learning and neuron-interpretation maps falls from 0.69 at expansion factor 2 to 0.10 at 64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forward concept-to-latent and reverse latent-to-concept assignments in SAEs disagree, less so in wider SAEs.

record.problems: The experiments use controlled two-dimensional synthetic data rather than LLM activations. The paper reports best concept-learning metrics across 10 random seeds, but gives no uncertainty intervals in the reported text. Some results are described only qualitatively or in figures. The authors describe their empirical study of the concept-learning–interpretation relationship as preliminary.
record.rows_left_out: No additional primary results relevant to the tested version were omitted. Detailed table cells for disagreement by concept type, task, architecture, and F1 interval are not cataloged separately because this measure does not directly test any listed version; the aggregate All row across expansion factors is included.

untested.parts: All: no model with more sparse features than dimensions, no near-orthogonal overlapping directions, no sparsity phase transition, no geometry.
All: no model neurons under capacity pressure, no feature importance or competition. SAE width effects on concept F1 are not a test.
All: no alternative causes of polysemanticity are examined.
All: no LLM activations; only 2-D synthetic data.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of SAE features in a model are not tested. The synthetic data are not a model's representation.
The dimensionality of superposed features is not tested. Multi-neuron units are halfspace intersections for cluster shapes, not multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1–R12 to V2 on the basis of the word 'capacity', but the study's capacity concerns the size of the SAE dictionary, not features competing inside a model. The reader's V2 supports and limits_scope labels are removed. Best-of-10-seed reporting and the absence of uncertainty estimates are further caveats.

versions.untested_parts: No test of more sparse features than dimensions, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent geometric transitions, or regular superposition geometry.

The study tests concept-learning capacity and neuron budgets, but not feature importance, prioritization of important features, or competition between a specified set of sparse features for dedicated dimensions versus sharing.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemantic neurons are evidence for superposition.
No LLM activations, feature-spread measurements in LLMs, or SAE recovery of LLM features.
No test of SAE feature completeness, stability across training runs or dictionaries, or canonical status.
The paper compares single-neuron and multi-neuron concept units, but does not test the dimensionality of features involved in superposition.

rows.subject: Theoretical SAE capacity
rows.operation_detail: Derives a necessary capacity bound for perfect monosemanticity when each concept uses at most kc neurons.
rows.note: A theoretical capacity bound, not a measurement from a trained network.
rows.check: A derived counting bound on SAE width needed for injective concept-to-unit maps. It is theory, not a measurement, and does not test why a model's neurons are polysemantic. It should not be linked to V2.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates a single-neuron unit on a neuron-separable synthetic concept.
rows.note: A single neuron suffices for this particular synthetic concept.
rows.check: F1 = 1.0 for a single SAE neuron on a separable 2-D cluster measures SAE concept alignment, not capacity-driven polysemanticity. Unlink from V2.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares a single neuron with a multi-neuron unit on a non-neuron-separable but unit-separable synthetic concept.
rows.note: The multi-neuron unit substantially improves performance but is not reported as perfect.
rows.check: Single neuron vs 4-neuron unit (F1 0.4144 to 0.8529) tests the halfspace-intersection geometry of SAE units, not feature competition for limited dimensions. Unlink from V2.

rows.subject: Top-K SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares a single neuron with a multi-neuron unit on a non-neuron-separable but unit-separable synthetic concept.
rows.note: The multi-neuron unit approaches perfect F1.
rows.check: Same issue as R3 (Top-K, F1 0.4559 to 0.9646). Unlink from V2.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares a single neuron with a multi-neuron unit for an easier-to-approximate synthetic concept.
rows.note: The larger unit improves approximation, but does not reach perfect F1.
rows.check: Concept-approximation F1 (0.710 to 0.9281) is about SAE unit shape, not a V2 mechanism. Unlink.

rows.subject: Top-K SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares a single neuron with a multi-neuron unit for an easier-to-approximate synthetic concept.
rows.note: The larger unit improves approximation, but does not reach perfect F1.
rows.check: Same issue as R5 (Top-K, F1 0.7815 to 0.9089). Unlink.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares a single neuron with a multi-neuron unit for a harder-to-approximate synthetic concept.
rows.note: The multi-neuron unit improves F1, but the result remains substantially below the easier approximation case.
rows.check: Approximation F1 on a heavily overlapping concept (0.2829 to 0.6261) is SAE concept alignment. Unlink from V2.

rows.subject: Top-K SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares single-neuron and multi-neuron performance for a harder-to-approximate synthetic concept.
rows.value: The best multi-neuron unit is substantially higher than any single neuron, but remains below the easier approximation case.
rows.note: The text does not give the F1 values for this comparison.
rows.check: No numeric values are stated (figure only). The row is SAE concept alignment, not V2. Unlink.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Varies SAE expansion factor and measures best concept-learning F1 at fixed L0.

conditions.value: fixed; individual values not stated in the prose

rows.value: Substantial improvement through expansion factor 16, then gains plateau.
rows.note: The prose reports the trend but not the individual F1 values.
rows.check: Best F1 rising with SAE expansion factor reflects a larger candidate pool in the dictionary. It is not evidence about a model's capacity causing polysemanticity. Unlink from V2.

rows.subject: Top-K SAE
rows.operation_detail: Varies SAE expansion factor and measures best concept-learning F1 at fixed L0.

conditions.value: fixed; individual values not stated in the prose

rows.value: F1 improves with expansion factor and plateaus; the plateau is clearer than for ReLU SAEs.
rows.note: The prose reports the trend but not the individual F1 values.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE and Top-K SAE
rows.operation_detail: Compares best concept-learning F1 across concept overlap and neuron-selection budget.
rows.value: Disjoint concepts have higher peak F1 than overlapping concepts; at fixed expansion factor, larger L0 generally improves F1.
rows.note: The statement applies to the reported synthetic concept tasks; exact values are not stated in the prose.
rows.check: Effects of disjoint vs overlapping clusters and of L0 on SAE F1 are not a V2 measure. Unlink. The 'partial' state has no basis against V2.

rows.subject: ReLU SAE
rows.operation_detail: Reports the effect of forcing an exact number of selected neurons on concept-separation F1.
rows.note: The paper also reports that forcing one extra neuron on the same 4-neuron unit makes F1 drop to 0.0924.
rows.check: An artifact of exact-N neuron selection (0.8529 vs 0.6748; 0.0924 when one neuron is forced in). It concerns the study's own selection procedure and should not be a V2 row.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Synthetic 2D concept tasks, including concept separation and approximation
reader_labels.reason: The capacity bound and experiments show that available neuron budgets and larger SAE candidate pools can improve concept representation; multi-neuron units substantially outperform single neurons on several concepts (R1, R3-R7, R9-R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Harder overlapping concepts and exact-size unit selection
reader_labels.reason: Multi-neuron gains are incomplete for harder approximation cases, and exact-N F1 can decrease when additional neurons are selected (R7, R8, R12).
